moduleTitle: SQE1 · Wills and Administration of Estates
title: Testamentary capacity and knowledge and approval
subtitle: The Banks v Goodfellow test, and when the presumption of a valid will breaks down
objectives: State the four-part Banks v Goodfellow test for testamentary capacity and explain what each limb requires
Explain when the presumption of knowledge and approval arises, and identify the circumstances — particularly beneficiary involvement in preparing the will — that displace it
Apply both doctrines to a fact pattern and identify which one is actually in issue

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the four-limb common law test for testamentary capacity
Knowledge and approval must be affirmatively proved where a solicitor-beneficiary drafts the will
Confirms Banks v Goodfellow, not the Mental Capacity Act 2005, remains the test for testamentary capacity

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Capacity and knowledge and approval are the two doctrines examiners most often blur together in a single fact pattern, because both can be triggered by the same facts — an elderly, unwell testator and a will that favours the person who helped write it. Where the profile shows the two are being confused, this note appears: 'These are two separate gates. A testator can have full capacity and still have a will fail for want of knowledge and approval, and vice versa.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know both tests well on paper. The test pool below leans on fact patterns that require you to work out which gate is actually being attacked — capacity, approval, or both.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 2 and get the four Banks v Goodfellow limbs solid before moving on — everything else in this lesson assumes you can list them without hesitation.

overview.hook: An elderly widow, three months before her death, rewrites her will to leave almost everything to the solicitor who drew it up for her, cutting her children out entirely. Nothing about the document is forged, and nobody disputes that she signed it. Whether it stands or falls turns on two separate questions most people never think to separate: did she have the mental capacity to make a will at all, and — quite apart from that — did she actually know and approve of what was in it?
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. There has been genuine judicial debate about whether the Mental Capacity Act 2005 has displaced the common law Banks v Goodfellow test for testamentary capacity. Recent Court of Appeal and High Court authority (including Clitheroe v Bond [2021] EWHC 1102 (Ch)) confirms Banks v Goodfellow remains the applicable test, and this lesson teaches it on that settled footing — but be aware the point has been litigated more than once and is not merely historical.

parts.heading: Two gates, not one
parts.voice: structural — frames the two doctrines before either is explained in depth
body: A valid will has to clear two separate hurdles that are easy to collapse into one another. The first is testamentary capacity: did the testator have the mental ability, at the relevant time, to make a will at all? The second is knowledge and approval: quite apart from mental capacity, did the testator actually know what was in the document and approve of its contents?

Most wills clear both without anyone asking the question — a rational-looking will, properly signed, by a testator nobody doubts, raises a presumption that both are satisfied. The doctrines only surface when something about the facts looks wrong: a testator whose mind may have been failing, or a will shaped by someone who stood to gain from writing it.

Keep the two questions apart as you work through this lesson. An exam fact pattern will often present symptoms consistent with both — old age, illness, a will that departs from what everyone expected — and expect you to work out which doctrine, or both, is actually engaged.

components.definition: The testator's mental ability, assessed at the relevant time, to understand the nature and effect of making a will — a separate question from whether the testator knew and approved of this particular will's contents.

interaction.prompt: A testator with full mental capacity signs a will she has never read, believing it to be a different document. Is capacity the doctrine in issue?
options: No — this is a knowledge and approval problem, not a capacity problem
Yes — she cannot have capacity if she didn't read the will
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Capacity is about mental ability in the abstract; here the problem is that she never knew what the document actually said — that's knowledge and approval.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what's actually wrong on these facts. Nothing suggests her mind was impaired — the problem is that she didn't know what she was signing, which is a knowledge and approval issue, not a capacity one.

parts.heading: The Banks v Goodfellow test
parts.voice: structural — a reference part students will return to before the exam
body: Banks v Goodfellow, decided in 1870, remains the test for testamentary capacity in England and Wales, and it hasn't been displaced by the Mental Capacity Act 2005 — the two operate side by side, but it is the older common law test that governs whether a will stands or falls.

The test has four limbs, and a testator must satisfy all four at the relevant time. Learn them as a checklist: an exam question will typically supply facts engaging one limb clearly while leaving the others merely assumed, and you're expected to notice which limb is actually doing the work.

The fourth limb is the one that trips people up, because it isn't really about intelligence or memory at all — it's about whether some disorder of the mind is actively distorting the testator's judgment about who should benefit, even if their general reasoning otherwise seems sound.

components.label: The four Banks v Goodfellow limbs
points: Understand the nature of the act of making a will and its broad effects
Understand the extent of the property of which they are disposing
Be able to comprehend and appreciate the claims to which they ought to give effect — who might expect to benefit, and why
Be free of any disorder of the mind that poisons their affections, perverts their sense of right, or produces an insane delusion influencing how the property is disposed of

components.factsShort: A testator suffering from delusions (including a belief he was pursued by an evil spirit) left his estate to his niece; the delusions were unconnected to the terms of the will.
components.ratioShort: A testator may have capacity despite suffering from insane delusions, provided those delusions do not affect or distort the actual disposition made in the will.

expanded.facts: John Banks suffered from delusions, including a fixed belief that he was being pursued by an imaginary man and by evil spirits. Despite this, he left his property to his niece, Margaret Goodfellow, who had lived with and cared for him. After his death, a nephew challenged the will on the ground that Banks lacked testamentary capacity because of his delusions.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Cockburn CJ held that it is essential a testator shall understand the nature of the act and its effects, understand the extent of the property, be able to comprehend and appreciate the claims to which he ought to give effect, and that no disorder of the mind shall poison his affections, pervert his sense of right, or bring about a disposal which, if his mind had been sound, would not have been made.
expanded.significance: The case establishes that delusions do not automatically destroy capacity — what matters is whether the delusion has actually influenced the will's contents. Banks's delusions about spirits had nothing to do with his niece or his property, so the will was upheld.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states the fourth limb of the Banks v Goodfellow test.
interaction.passage: It is essential that a testator shall understand the nature of the act and its effects, and shall understand the extent of the property of which he is disposing. He must also be able to comprehend and appreciate the claims to which he ought to give effect. With a view to this latter object, no disorder of the mind shall poison his affections, pervert his sense of right, or prevent the exercise of his natural faculties — no insane delusion shall influence his will in disposing of his property and bring about a disposal of it which, if the mind had been sound, would not have been made.
interaction.ratioSentence: With a view to this latter object, no disorder of the mind shall poison his affections, pervert his sense of right, or prevent the exercise of his natural faculties — no insane delusion shall influence his will in disposing of his property and bring about a disposal of it which, if the mind had been sound, would not have been made.

parts.heading: The presumption of knowledge and approval, and what breaks it
parts.voice: direct — sets out the default rule before showing how it fails
body: Once capacity, due execution and rationality on the face of the will are established, the law presumes the testator knew and approved of its contents — you don't normally have to prove a testator read every clause; the presumption does the work.

That presumption can be rebutted, and the paradigm case is where a beneficiary was involved in preparing the will — drafting it, giving the instructions, or otherwise shaping its terms — particularly where that person takes a substantial benefit under it. Suspicion doesn't automatically defeat the will, but it shifts the burden: the person seeking to prove the will (the propounder) must now affirmatively show the testator actually knew and approved of the contents, rather than relying on the presumption.

This is where solicitors have to be especially careful. A solicitor who drafts a will under which they, or their family, take a significant gift is exactly the scenario the doctrine exists to catch — however honestly the solicitor believes they acted.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that if the testator clearly had capacity, knowledge and approval is automatically satisfied too.
components.whyItsWrong: Capacity and knowledge and approval are independent requirements. A fully capacitous testator can still have a will fail for want of knowledge and approval if suspicious circumstances — most commonly, a beneficiary's hand in drafting — are not affirmatively answered by the propounder.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact most likely to rebut the presumption of knowledge and approval here.
interaction.scenarioText: Harold, an elderly widower with full mental capacity, asks his solicitor to prepare a new will. The solicitor drafts the will, under which the solicitor personally receives a substantial cash legacy, and Harold signs it after a brief meeting without it being read aloud to him.
tappableSpans: the solicitor personally receives a substantial cash legacy
signs it after a brief meeting
interaction.correctSpan: the solicitor personally receives a substantial cash legacy
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the trigger. A solicitor drafting a will under which they personally benefit is the classic suspicious circumstance — it shifts the burden onto the propounder to prove Harold actually knew and approved of the gift, rather than relying on the usual presumption.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Age and full capacity aren't the issue here — the presumption is triggered by the solicitor drafting a will that benefits themselves personally. That relationship is what a court treats as suspicious.

parts.heading: Wintle v Nye: the burden actually being discharged
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks through the facts before drawing the principle
body: Wintle v Nye is the leading illustration of what happens when the presumption is displaced and the propounder has to prove knowledge and approval affirmatively — and fails to.

Mr Nye, a solicitor, prepared a will for an elderly, unworldly spinster, Miss Wells, under which he received the overwhelming bulk of a substantial estate. The circumstances were suspicious on their face: the solicitor had drafted the document, he was its principal beneficiary, and there was real doubt about how far Miss Wells had actually grasped the scale and effect of what she was signing.

The House of Lords upheld the trial judge's conclusion that Nye had failed to discharge the burden the law placed on him. It was not enough that Miss Wells had signed a document that looked formally valid — the propounder had to affirmatively satisfy the court that she truly knew and approved the contents, and on these facts he could not.

components.title: Knowledge and approval: from presumption to proof
components.description: How the burden shifts once suspicious circumstances appear.

nodes.label: Will is duly executed and appears rational on its face
Presumption of knowledge and approval arises — no further proof normally needed
Suspicious circumstances appear (e.g. beneficiary drafted the will, or was closely involved)
Burden shifts to the propounder to affirmatively prove actual knowledge and approval
If the propounder cannot discharge that burden, the will (or the suspicious gift) fails

components.textAlternative: Ordinarily, a duly executed will that looks rational on its face carries a presumption of knowledge and approval. Where suspicious circumstances appear — most commonly a beneficiary's involvement in drafting — that presumption is displaced, and the burden shifts to whoever is propounding the will to affirmatively prove the testator actually knew and approved of its contents. If they cannot, the will, or the tainted gift within it, fails.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that, once suspicious circumstances arise, it is enough for the propounder simply to show the will was properly signed and witnessed?
sliderLabels: Not sufficient — actual knowledge and approval must be proved
interaction.correctPosition: Not sufficient — actual knowledge and approval must be proved
interaction.explanation: Wintle v Nye shows formal validity is not enough once suspicion is raised. The propounder must go further and affirmatively prove the testator's actual knowledge and approval of the contents, not merely that the paperwork was correct.

parts.heading: Putting the two doctrines together
parts.voice: Socratic — works through a combined fact pattern
body: Real exam questions rarely label which doctrine is in play — they give you a testator, some facts about their health or circumstances, and a will that looks odd in some way, and leave you to work out whether capacity, knowledge and approval, or both, are actually at issue.

A useful discipline: ask first whether anything suggests the testator's mind, at the relevant time, could not satisfy all four Banks v Goodfellow limbs. Then, separately, ask whether anything about how the will was prepared — who drafted it, who benefits, how it was explained — raises suspicion requiring proof of actual knowledge and approval. The two answers can point in different directions.

Consider a testator recovering from a stroke, whose son — the will's main beneficiary — sits in on the meeting with the solicitor and answers most of the testator's questions for her. Capacity might well be intact if her cognition has recovered; but the son's active involvement is exactly the kind of suspicious circumstance that puts knowledge and approval, not capacity, at the centre of the analysis.

components.text: Due execution under s 9 — considered in the next lesson — establishes that a document was properly signed and witnessed. It says nothing, on its own, about whether the testator had capacity or knew and approved the contents; those are separate questions this lesson has addressed.
elements: Due execution is necessary but not sufficient
Capacity and knowledge and approval sit alongside due execution as independent requirements

interaction.prompt: Deborah, aged 84, has mild dementia but lucid days. On a day her GP records as lucid, she instructs a will leaving her house to her carer, whom she has known for six months, and nothing to her estranged son. The carer was present throughout the meeting with the solicitor and later helped Deborah sign the will. Analyse whether the will is likely to be challenged successfully.
factsToOrder: Deborah has mild dementia but documented lucid days
Instructions given, and will signed, on a day recorded as lucid
The carer is the main beneficiary and has known Deborah only six months
The carer was present throughout the solicitor meeting and at signing

scaffolds.support: Issue and Rule given in full; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Deborah had testamentary capacity, and separately, whether the presumption of knowledge and approval is displaced by the carer's involvement.
modelAnswer.rule: Capacity is assessed under Banks v Goodfellow at the relevant time; a diagnosis of dementia does not itself defeat capacity if the four limbs are satisfied on a lucid day. Knowledge and approval is presumed for a rational, duly executed will, but that presumption is displaced by suspicious circumstances such as a substantial beneficiary's close involvement in the will's preparation, per Wintle v Nye.
modelAnswer.application: Capacity is likely to be defensible: the instructions and execution occurred on a documented lucid day, and nothing suggests a delusion distorting her view of her son or the carer. Knowledge and approval is the stronger ground of challenge: the carer, a recent acquaintance and the main beneficiary, was present throughout instructions and signing — a suspicious circumstance requiring the carer (or whoever propounds the will) to affirmatively prove Deborah's actual knowledge and approval, which the facts as given do not establish.
modelAnswer.conclusion: A capacity challenge is unlikely to succeed on these facts, but a knowledge and approval challenge has real prospects given the carer's proximity to the drafting and execution process.

testPool.prompt: A testator's solicitor wants to confirm the correct legal test for testamentary capacity before taking instructions. Which case supplies that test?
options: Banks v Goodfellow (1870)
Wintle v Nye (1959)
Re Estate of Park (1954)
Mental Capacity Act 2005, s 2 only
testPool.explanation: Banks v Goodfellow remains the applicable common law test for testamentary capacity, confirmed as still governing even after the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is one of the four Banks v Goodfellow limbs?
options: Understanding the extent of the property being disposed of
Being over the age of 21
Having the will independently witnessed by a doctor
Having made a previous will
testPool.explanation: Understanding the extent of the property is the second limb. The other options are not part of the capacity test at all.

testPool.prompt: A testator has a fixed but false belief that he is being watched by a foreign government, unrelated to his family or estate. On Banks v Goodfellow, is his capacity automatically defeated?
options: No — a delusion only defeats capacity if it actually distorts the disposition made in the will
Yes — any delusion of any kind automatically defeats capacity
Yes, but only if the delusion is about money
No — delusions are never relevant to capacity
testPool.explanation: Banks v Goodfellow itself involved a testator with unrelated delusions whose will was upheld. What matters under the fourth limb is whether the disorder has actually poisoned the testator's judgment about who should benefit.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor is asked to draft a will for a client who, during the meeting, cannot explain roughly what her estate consists of or name any of her close relatives even when prompted. Which limb of Banks v Goodfellow is most obviously in doubt?
options: Understanding the extent of the property, and comprehending the claims of those who might expect to benefit
Freedom from an insane delusion only
Understanding the nature of the act of making a will only
None — capacity is presumed regardless of what she can explain
testPool.explanation: Failing to grasp the extent of the estate and failing to identify people with a claim on it go directly to the second and third limbs of the test.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best states the effect of the presumption of knowledge and approval?
options: Once a will is duly executed and appears rational on its face, the testator is presumed to have known and approved its contents unless that presumption is displaced
A testator must always be asked to read every clause of a will aloud before signing
Knowledge and approval is only relevant if the testator lacked capacity
The presumption can never be rebutted once a will is signed
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to think capacity and knowledge and approval rise and fall together, but they are independent doctrines — and the presumption described here is rebuttable, not absolute.
testPool.explanation: The presumption exists precisely so that ordinary, unremarkable wills do not require detailed proof of what the testator understood — but suspicious circumstances can and do displace it.

testPool.prompt: What did Wintle v Nye actually decide?
options: That a solicitor-beneficiary who prepared the will had failed to discharge the burden of proving the testatrix's actual knowledge and approval
That solicitors can never be beneficiaries under wills they draft
That the testatrix lacked testamentary capacity
That due execution under s 9 was not satisfied
testPool.trapExplanation: Wintle v Nye is not a capacity case, and it does not create a blanket bar on solicitor-beneficiaries — it turns on the propounder's failure to prove actual knowledge and approval once suspicion was raised.
testPool.explanation: The House of Lords upheld the finding that Nye, as the drafting solicitor and principal beneficiary, had not affirmatively proved that Miss Wells knew and approved of the will's contents.

testPool.prompt: A testator with no history of illness makes a straightforward will leaving her estate equally between her three children, drafted by an independent solicitor with no interest in the estate. A disappointed distant cousin wants to challenge it for want of knowledge and approval. What is the strongest advice?
options: The presumption of knowledge and approval applies and there are no suspicious circumstances to rebut it, so a challenge on this ground is very unlikely to succeed
A challenge will automatically succeed because any family member can challenge any will
The will is void because the solicitor did not personally witness execution
Knowledge and approval cannot apply because the testator had full capacity
testPool.trapExplanation: Full capacity does not exempt a will from the knowledge and approval analysis — it simply happens that, on these facts, nothing rebuts the ordinary presumption, so the outcome favours the will rather than the challenger.
testPool.explanation: With an independent drafter, no beneficiary involvement in preparation, and a rational-looking distribution, there is nothing to displace the presumption. The distant cousin's challenge has no suspicious circumstance to point to.

testPool.prompt: An 89-year-old testator with a recent diagnosis of early-stage dementia gives instructions for a will on a day her solicitor records as lucid and coherent, correctly identifying her assets and family. She signs it the same day. Is her capacity likely to be upheld?
options: Yes — a diagnosis of dementia does not itself defeat capacity where the Banks v Goodfellow limbs are satisfied at the relevant time
No — any dementia diagnosis automatically defeats testamentary capacity
No — capacity can only be assessed by a court, never by a solicitor's contemporaneous note
Yes, but only if she has a formal court declaration of capacity beforehand
testPool.explanation: Capacity is assessed at the relevant time by reference to the four limbs, not by diagnosis alone. A lucid-day assessment properly documented supports capacity being upheld.

testPool.prompt: A testator's adult daughter drives him to the solicitor's office, sits in on the meeting, prompts him with answers, and is left a legacy far larger than his other children's. The will otherwise appears formally valid. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The presumption of knowledge and approval is displaced, and the daughter (or whoever propounds the will) must affirmatively prove his actual knowledge and approval
Nothing — driving a parent to an appointment is never legally significant
The will is automatically void for undue influence without further inquiry
The daughter's presence is irrelevant because the testator signed the will himself
testPool.explanation: Close involvement by a substantially benefiting relative in giving instructions is a recognised suspicious circumstance under the Wintle v Nye line of authority, shifting the burden onto the propounder.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor is asked by an existing client to draft a will under which the solicitor's own spouse will receive a significant legacy. What is the best practical advice?
options: Have the will drafted and witnessed independently of the solicitor and their firm, and keep a clear record of the testator's instructions, to avoid the suspicion that undermined the will in Wintle v Nye
Proceed as normal, since only the solicitor personally benefiting (not a spouse) is legally significant
Refuse to act only if the legacy exceeds a fixed statutory amount
No special precautions are needed provided the will is signed in the solicitor's presence
testPool.explanation: A benefit to a solicitor's spouse raises the same suspicious-circumstance concern as a direct benefit to the solicitor. Independent drafting and a clear instructions record are the standard safeguards against a Wintle v Nye-style challenge.

testPool.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes testamentary capacity from knowledge and approval as separate legal requirements for a valid will?
options: Capacity asks whether the testator had the mental ability to make a will at all; knowledge and approval asks whether the testator actually knew and approved of this particular document's contents
They are the same requirement described in different words
Capacity is only relevant to gifts of land; knowledge and approval is only relevant to gifts of money
Knowledge and approval is presumed only if capacity is in doubt
testPool.explanation: The two doctrines protect against different risks — an incapable testator, and a capable testator who did not truly know or approve of a document propounded as their will — and a fact pattern can raise either, both, or neither.

testPool.prompt: What is the effect of a testator having lucid intervals despite an underlying degenerative illness, for the purposes of testamentary capacity?
options: Capacity is assessed at the relevant time, so a will made during a genuinely lucid interval can be valid despite the underlying illness
Lucid intervals are legally irrelevant once any degenerative diagnosis exists
A will made during a lucid interval is automatically invalid unless a doctor is also present
Capacity must be reassessed by a court before any such will can take effect
testPool.explanation: Banks v Goodfellow capacity is time-specific. A properly evidenced lucid interval can support a valid will notwithstanding a later or surrounding decline.

testPool.prompt: A will leaves the entire estate to a next-door neighbour who has no prior relationship of care or friendship with the testator, and who typed the will himself on the testator's computer before bringing it round for signature. What issue does this most obviously raise?
options: Knowledge and approval, given the beneficiary's direct hand in preparing the document
Testamentary capacity, because neighbours can never be trusted beneficiaries
Due execution only, because the will was typed rather than handwritten
No issue at all, since neighbours are as entitled to benefit as anyone else
testPool.explanation: A beneficiary preparing the will themselves, especially absent any prior close relationship, is a textbook suspicious circumstance requiring proof of actual knowledge and approval — a typed document is not inherently a due execution problem.

testPool.prompt: Has the Mental Capacity Act 2005 replaced Banks v Goodfellow as the test for testamentary capacity?
options: No — recent authority confirms Banks v Goodfellow remains the applicable common law test for testamentary capacity
Yes — the 2005 Act's statutory test has fully replaced the common law test for wills
The two tests apply only in Scotland and are irrelevant in England and Wales
The MCA 2005 abolished testamentary capacity as a requirement entirely
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to assume a modern statute automatically supersedes an 1870 common law rule, but the courts have specifically addressed and rejected that assumption in this area.
testPool.explanation: Case law, including Clitheroe v Bond, has confirmed that Banks v Goodfellow continues to govern testamentary capacity notwithstanding the MCA 2005's general statutory framework.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating capacity and knowledge and approval as one question. They are separate gates with separate tests, separate burdens, and separate leading cases — a fact pattern can fail on either, both, or neither, and the exam expects you to say which.
